catalog_quote: First, all lexical words have lexical prominence or primary stress (‘obligatoriness parameter’) with one syllable bearing the highest degree of prominence – ‘culminativity parameter’ (Hyman 2006). Second, stressed vowels are longer than unstressed vowels. As previously mentioned, glottalized vowels always occur under stress and are double the duration of modal vowels, hence my analysis of them as bimoraic. sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are by Analía Gutiérrez and were obtained and read. (1) The 2015 UBC dissertation (already listed; UBC's live host blocks our network, but a 22 MB Internet Archive copy of the cIRcle PDF was downloaded) contains the full stress analysis (ch. 4, pp. 153-213): quantity-sensitive iambic system, moraic /ʔ/, final stress in disyllabic roots, primary stress on the rightmost foot of the Prosodic Word, morphological-edge alignment; it confirms the catalog's classification and is the primary behind the JIPA deciding quote. (2) The 2016 LIAMES glottal-stop paper (open access, not previously listed) is about the prosodic parsing of /ʔ/; its only stress content is the Weight-to-Stress licensing of glottalized vowels and a footnote summarizing the dissertation, so it confirms but adds nothing. Bonus: Stell's 1987 UBA doctoral grammar (the source behind the surveys' transmitted alternating row, cited 'Stell 1989' by Gutiérrez) is openly available at repositorio.filo.uba.ar and was downloaded (2 vols., scanned text, page scan of pp. 81-83 checked): primary stress is root-final 'con una frecuencia mayor', shifted by suffixes; secondary stress on the 2nd and 4th syllable from the left in 4+ syllable words, with no weight statement. That closes most of the compilers note's 'Stell pin': the survey's 'odd-numbered from R' alternation is not what Stell describes (she counts from the left, hedged), and Gutiérrez rejects her secondary-stress data. Stell 1972 (Fonología de la lengua Axluxlaj) remains unlocated online. No change to the catalog's classification is indicated; the dissertation and Stell 1987 should be added as corroborating/refining sources. and.

new_statements.quote: In this section, I consider the different word-stress patterns in Nivaĉle and propose that (i) the foot type is iambic, and (ii) the Nivaĉle language has a quantity-sensitive stress system, where the moraic weight of /ʔ/ is consistently correlated with stress prominence, and (iii) a CVC syllable in word initial position – and only in this position of convergent morphological and prosodic prominence – is stressed [...] Main stress falls on the rightmost foot of the Prosodic Word. [...] Turning our attention to disyllabic roots, the basic generalization is that stress is final, motivating the claim that the stress system of Nivaĉle is right-headed, or iambic.

new_statements.reading: Word-level, culminative primary stress assigned by quantity-sensitive iambic footing: only vowels and the postvocalic glottal stop are moraic (coda consonants are not), glottalized/glottal-coda syllables are heavy and always stressed, disyllabic roots are otherwise final-stressed, primary stress sits on the rightmost foot of the Prosodic Word, foot parsing is aligned to morphological edges (root/stem/word right edge; possessive-prefix left edge), and an initial CVC can take secondary stress. Rightward-alternating secondaries are not described; the alternation in the surveys traces to Stell 1987:83 (2nd and 4th syllable from the left), which Gutiérrez disputes (pp. 156-158). This is the same author's fuller primary analysis of what the catalog's deciding JIPA statement condenses; it supports the weight-conditioned (weight-hedged / weight-sensitive) coding and adds the explicit rightmost-foot rule.

Cuando un nombre va precedido por un determinante básico (4.1.1.), los dos forman una unidad acentual: [p. 54] … La única excepción a este esquema de acentuación es cuando una palabra contiene el sufijo -c’oya (5.4.3.), que atrae el acento principal en su primera sílaba: [p. 55] … 2.8.2. El tono tiende a subir un poco en las vocales acentuadas. [p. 55]
new_statements.translation: 2.8.1. Word stress. The main stress of the Nivacle word regularly falls on the last syllable. When a noun is preceded by a basic determiner (4.1.1.), the two form a single accentual unit: [p. 54] … The only exception to this stress scheme is when a word contains the suffix -c’oya (5.4.3.), which attracts the main stress onto its first syllable: [p. 55] … 2.8.2. Secondary stress and phrase stress. As a general rule, grammatical words attach to the nucleus to form an accentual unit with one main stress and secondary stress(es). Pitch tends to rise a little on stressed vowels. [p. 55]

new_statements.relation_note: Same primary placement as the catalog's StressTyp2 rule (alternating stress from the right: final primary) and as the final default in the existing Gutiérrez 2015 statement (rightmost iamb). It gives no support to the catalog's iterative alternating secondaries: secondary stress is a phrase/accentual-unit phenomenon with secondaries on root syllables. Relative to Gutiérrez's weight-sensitive analysis it is compatible on the default but silent on glottalized-vowel weight, and its wording ('regularmente', 'la única excepción') is firmer than Gutiérrez's and than Fabre's own 2016 revision.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls regularly on the last syllable of the word. The accentual unit is often larger than the lexical word (determiner + noun; negative ni, indefinite-subject prefix chi and the subordinators ti / ca + verb; the diminutive clitic =lh-ôs with its host, p. 113 'se pronuncia como una sola palabra, con acento final'), and the primary still lands on the unit's final syllable: na yijpôyich [najxpɒwˈˈjiʧ] 'my house', ni nastô’ya [ninastɒʔˈˈja] 'I don't know', ca chinasclanjulh [qaʧinaskl͡anˈˈxuɬ] 'that they be respected'; a dependent verb joined to the main clause carries the primary on its last syllable (papi vô’mesh ti yen [papivɒʔˈˈmeʃtijen]). Stress is presented as a phonetic property (pitch rises a little on stressed vowels; glottalized vowels get an echo vowel in stressed syllables of slow speech, p. 45); nothing on contrast or on syllable weight.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Described only at the level of the accentual unit / phrase (§2.8.2, p. 55): grammatical words join the nucleus into one unit 'con un acento principal y acento(s) secundario(s)'; the vowel of a secondary-stressed syllable may optionally lengthen, and in longer utterances some secondary-stressed syllables lengthen their vowel (p. 56). The transcriptions put secondaries on lexical-root syllables rather than on an alternating count: [ˈɬxu:naʃˈˈxuɬ] 'it is like…', [papiniɬˈkutsfaˈˈsa] 'their enemies', [ˈʔampapukantɒʔˈˈjiʃ] 'nobody knows', [kadjosˈɬa:siˈˈnok] 'the word of God', [tʔaˈxu:japapineˈka:kuˈxanxasˈˈa] 'for the believers' (secondaries on syllables 2, 7, 9 of 11). No iterative odd-from-the-right rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: 'La única excepción': the suffix -c’oya (5.4.3.) attracts main stress onto its own first syllable, asclanelh’ôcjiyic’oya [askl͡aneɬʔɒkxiˈˈkʔoja] 'prepare it for us!'; restated p. 184: 'Una particularidad prosódica única de -c’oya es que el acento principal del verbo recae en la primera sílaba del sufijo.' No other exceptions in this 2014 edition. (The author's 2016 revision of the same grammar, already held by the project from the weight-sensitive tier pass at, §2.8.1 pp. 78-80, softens this to 'recae generalmente en la última sílaba. No es distintivo', adds glottalized /ɒ̰/ and /a/ before /m/ attracting stress, loanwords and penult-stressed derived forms, and cites Gutiérrez 2015: 166.)
new_statements.identity_note: Fabre 2014 describes Nivacle (Nivaclé / Chulupí) of the Paraguayan Chaco without naming a dialect; examples are in the Catholic and Mennonite orthographies with IPA. The existing Gutiérrez statement is on the shichaam lhavos variety and Stell 1987 (already held by the project) on Axluxlaj; all fall under niva1238.

readall_conflicts: Fabre 2014 states fixed final primary stress with a single suffixal exception (-c’oya), whereas the existing statement (Gutiérrez 2015, with her 2016 JIPA and 2019 Cuadernos papers behind the weight-sensitive tier record) analyses a quantity-sensitive iambic system in which a glottalized (bimoraic) penult takes the primary (xiˈβeʔk͡lə 'moon') and possessive-prefixed inalienable nouns can be penult-stressed (ji-ˈka-saʃ). The two share the final default but differ in type (fixed vs weight-sensitive) and in the inventory of exceptions. Fabre's own 2016 revision of the same grammar (held by the project, §2.8.1 pp. 78-80) retreats from the 2014 wording to 'generalmente … No es distintivo', adds glottalized /ɒ̰/ attracting stress, loanword and penult-stressed derived forms ('quedan muchas interrogantes'), and cites Gutiérrez 2015: 166, so the 2014 'regularmente / la única excepción' statement is the author's earlier, simpler description rather than a considered rebuttal of the weight analysis. Neither Fabre edition nor Gutiérrez supports the StressTyp2 secondary string (alternating odd syllables from the right): Fabre 2014's secondaries sit on lexical-root syllables inside phrase-sized accentual units, and Gutiérrez's only secondary is an initial CVC foot; that part of the catalog rule remains unsupported by every readable source.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding JIPA quotation is verbatim in the extracted text we hold at p. 413 'Stress' section, exactly where the locator says; the Cuadernos 2019 and Fabre 2016 corroborating passages are also present in copies we hold. (2) Deciding source: a JIPA Illustration (2016 online / 2019 print) with instrumental duration data, written by the author of the 2015 UBC phonology dissertation on this language; corroborated by the held 542-pp Fabre 2016 grammar (final stress 'generalmente', non-distinctive, glottalized /ɒ̰/ attracts stress) — all consistent with the catalog's right-edge iambic, weight(=glottalization)-sensitive, 'weight-hedged' coding. Two further open Gutiérrez papers downloaded now (WCCFL 33 2016 pp. 183-184; CJL 2020 p. 282) restate the same analysis and add the morphological edge-alignment detail (prefixed MSt2 forms align left, giving penult stress in ji-k͡lé.sa, ji-ʃín.βo)

sources.quote: 'Finally, Nivaĉle has a quantity-sensitive iambic stress system. There is a consistent correlation between bimoraic weight (tautosyllabic /Vʔ/) and stress prominence. In addition, primary/secondary stress patterns reflect competing edge-alignment constraints where prosodic foot domains align with internal morphological category (MCat) edges, specifically Root (Rt), Stem1 (St1), Stem2 (StressTyp2), and Morphological Word (MWd). For a fuller explanation of Nivaĉle stress assignment domains, see Gutiérrez (2015).'

sources.quote: given that there is a consistent correlation between glottalized vowels and the locus of stress, I propose that a postvocalic glottal stop is, like vowels, underlyingly moraic. Recall that the Weight-to-Stress Principle (Prince & Smolensky 1993) states that heavy (bimoraic) syllables are required to be stressed. (p. 18) [...] A superficially complex stress system in Nivaĉle is shown to reduce to systematic regularities of three types. First, it is shown that stress is quantity-sensitive, with a consistent correlation between bimoraic weight (tautosyllabic /Vʔ/) and stress prominence. Secondly, primary/secondary stress patterns reflect competing edge-alignment constraints where prosodic foot domains align with internal morphological category (MCat) edges. (fn. 6, p. 24)
sources.locator: p. 18 (§ on /Vʔ/ representation) and footnote 6, p. 24 (journal pagination 323-347)
sources.note: Paper is about the featural and prosodic parsing of the glottal stop (onset vs. complex nucleus vs. coda), not stress placement; stress appears only as the licensing condition for glottalized vowels (moraic /ʔ/, Weight-to-Stress) and in a footnote that summarizes the dissertation's three-part stress analysis and defers to Gutiérrez (2015). No new placement rule or examples of stress location beyond the dissertation.

Cuando las raíces son bisílabas o trisílabas el acento primario cae, con una frecuencia mayor, estadísticamente comprobada, en la última sílaba. En las construcciones morfológicas constituidas por raíces monosílabas y bisílabas la presencia de determinados sufijos de flexión y de derivación desplazan regularmente el acento primario a la última sílaba. En las construcciones morfológicas de cuatro o más sílabas el acento primario se mantiene, en general, en la raíz [...] (p. 81) b) El acento secundario cae en la segunda y cuarta sílaba de construcciones morfológicas de cuatro o más sílabas, siempre que no coincida con el acento primario (p. 83) — Translation: a) Primary stress falls on the root and on certain inflectional and derivational affixes.
